prompt: Which of these is not matter?

choices.text: A dream you had last night
The helium inside a party balloon
choices.why: Helium is a gas, but it still has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Gases are easy to forget, like air.

choices.text: A grain of sand
choices.why: A grain of sand has mass and takes up space, so it is matter.

choices.text: A glass of orange juice
choices.why: Orange juice has mass and takes up space, so it is matter.

explanation: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. A dream is a thought, and thoughts, ideas, emotions, and hopes are not matter.

prompt: Which of these is a chemical property of a sheet of paper?

choices.text: It burns when lit with a match
It is white
choices.why: Color describes the paper as it exists, so it is a physical property.

choices.text: It is a solid at room temperature
choices.why: Phase (solid, liquid, or gas) is a physical property.

choices.text: It is 28 centimeters long
choices.why: Size describes the paper as it exists, so it is a physical property.

explanation: Chemical properties describe how matter changes form in the presence of other matter, as when paper burns. Color, phase, and size describe matter as it exists: physical properties.

prompt: Which of these is a chemical change?

choices.text: An egg cooking in a frying pan
A puddle of water freezing into ice
choices.why: Freezing changes only the phase, from liquid to solid, so it is a physical change.

choices.text: A chocolate bar melting in the sun
choices.why: Melting changes the phase, not the chemical composition, so it is a physical change.

choices.text: A log being split into firewood
choices.why: Splitting changes size and shape, not what the wood is made of, so it is a physical change.

explanation: In a chemical change, the chemical composition changes and new forms of matter are made, as when an egg cooks. Freezing, melting, and cutting change only physical properties such as phase, size, and shape.

prompt: You stir sugar into hot tea until you can no longer see it. What kind of change is that?

choices.text: A physical change: the sugar and tea form a mixture
A chemical change, because the sugar seems to disappear
choices.why: The sugar is still there, mixed so finely that you can't see it, just as salt dissolved in water is still present.

choices.text: A chemical change, because the tea is hot
choices.why: Heat alone doesn't make a change chemical. What matters is whether the chemical composition changes and new substances form.

explanation: Dissolved sugar in tea is a homogeneous mixture, a physical combination of substances. The sugar's chemical composition doesn't change.

prompt: What makes a substance an element rather than a compound?

choices.text: It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means
It is a solid at room temperature
choices.why: Phase doesn't decide it: nonmetal elements, for instance, exist in a variety of phases at room temperature.

choices.text: It is found in nature
choices.why: Compounds such as water are found in nature too.

choices.text: It has the same properties throughout
choices.why: That's true of every substance, compounds included. An element is the simplest type of substance.

explanation: An element is the simplest type of chemical substance: it can't be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means. A compound is a combination of more than one element.

prompt: Table sugar is a single substance made of three elements: carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. What kind of matter is it?

choices.text: A compound
An element
choices.why: An element is the simplest type of substance and can't be broken down further. Sugar is made of three elements.

choices.text: A mixture
choices.why: A mixture is a physical combination of more than one substance. Sugar is one substance, with properties of its own.

explanation: A compound is a combination of more than one element, and it behaves as a completely different substance from its elements.

prompt: A bowl of cereal with milk is…

choices.text: A heterogeneous mixture
A homogeneous mixture
choices.why: In a homogeneous mixture you can't tell the substances apart, but here you can see the cereal and the milk separately.

choices.text: A compound
choices.why: The cereal and milk are only mixed physically; they don't combine into one new substance.

explanation: In a heterogeneous mixture it is easy to tell, sometimes by the naked eye, that more than one substance is present.

prompt: An element can be hammered into thin sheets, drawn into wires, and conducts electricity well. What is it?

choices.text: A metal
A nonmetal
choices.why: Nonmetals are brittle when solid, conduct electricity and heat poorly, and can't be made into sheets or wires.

choices.text: A semi-metal
choices.why: Semi-metals have some properties of metals and some of nonmetals; this element has all the metal properties listed.

explanation: Metals are malleable (they can be pounded into thin sheets), ductile (they can be drawn into thin wires), and conduct electricity and heat well.

prompt: Mercury is a liquid at room temperature. Is it a metal?

choices.text: Yes: it's the well-known exception to metals being solid at room temperature
No: metals are always solid at room temperature
choices.why: Almost all are, but mercury is the well-known exception.

choices.text: No: an element can't be a liquid
choices.why: Elements exist in different phases at room temperature; nonmetals, for example, come in a variety of phases.

explanation: At room temperature metals are solid, with mercury the well-known exception. It still has all the other expected properties of a metal.

prompt: A student says that air is not matter, because you can't see it. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Air is matter, because it has mass and takes up space
Air is not matter, because matter must be visible
choices.why: Being visible isn't part of the definition. Air is so thin that we forget it has mass and takes up space, but it does.

choices.text: Air is not matter, because it is a gas, not a solid
choices.why: Gas is one of the three phases of matter. The phase doesn't decide whether something is matter.

choices.text: Air is matter only when it is moving, as wind
choices.why: Air has mass and takes up space whether it is moving or still.

explanation: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Air is very thin compared with a book or a rock, but it still has mass and takes up space, so it is matter.

prompt: A chemist records four observations about a sample of an unknown element. Which one is a physical property?

choices.text: It is a shiny, silvery solid
It reacts violently when dropped into water
choices.why: This describes how the element changes form in the presence of other matter (water), so it is a chemical property.

choices.text: It burns when it is heated in air
choices.why: Whether a sample burns is a chemical property: it describes how the matter changes form in the presence of other matter.

choices.text: It slowly turns dull as it reacts with air
choices.why: Reacting with air turns the element into new matter, so this describes a chemical property.

explanation: Physical properties describe matter as it exists, such as its color, shape, and phase. Reacting with water or air and burning describe how the element changes form in the presence of other matter, so they are chemical properties.

prompt: Which statement describes a chemical property, rather than a chemical change?

choices.text: Dry wood is able to burn
The logs in the campfire are burning
choices.why: This is the burning actually happening, so it is a chemical change: the process of demonstrating the chemical property.

choices.text: The wood is brown and rough
choices.why: Color and texture describe the wood as it exists, so they are physical properties.

choices.text: The log was split into kindling
choices.why: Splitting changes only the size and shape of the wood, so it is a physical change.

explanation: A chemical property describes how matter can change form in the presence of other matter, such as being able to burn. A chemical change is the process of demonstrating that property, such as logs actually burning.

prompt: A chemist lists five characteristics of a sample: it is cube-shaped; it is gray; it is a solid at room temperature; it burns when lit; and it forms a new substance when left in moist air. How many of these five are physical properties?
explanation: Shape, color, and phase describe the sample as it exists, so 3 are physical properties. Burning and forming a new substance in moist air describe how it changes form in the presence of other matter, so those 2 are chemical properties.

prompt: Which of these is a physical change?

choices.text: Alcohol in a thermometer expanding as it warms
A match burning after it is struck
choices.why: Burning changes the chemical composition of the match and makes new forms of matter, so it is a chemical change.

choices.text: Food being digested in the stomach
choices.why: In digestion, food is chemically reacted so the body can absorb it. That is a chemical change.

choices.text: Pancake batter cooking on a hot griddle
choices.why: Cooking involves chemical changes: the heat turns the batter into new forms of matter.

explanation: When alcohol in a thermometer warms, only its volume changes; it is still alcohol. A physical change alters physical properties without affecting chemical composition.

prompt: Gasoline left in an open can slowly evaporates. Gasoline in a car engine burns. How should these two changes be classified?

choices.text: Evaporating is a physical change; burning is a chemical change
Evaporating is a chemical change; burning is a physical change
choices.why: This is reversed. Evaporating only changes the phase from liquid to gas, while burning makes new forms of matter.

choices.text: Both are physical changes, because the gasoline becomes a gas
choices.why: Burning doesn't just change the phase. It changes the chemical composition and makes new forms of matter.

choices.text: Both are chemical changes, because the gasoline disappears
choices.why: Evaporated gasoline is still gasoline, now in the gas phase. Disappearing from view doesn't mean its composition changed.

explanation: Evaporation changes only the phase of the gasoline, a physical property, so it is a physical change. Burning changes the gasoline's chemical composition into new forms of matter, so it is a chemical change.

prompt: A marshmallow held over a campfire turns black and crusty. A student says this must be a physical change, because only its color and texture changed. What is wrong with this reasoning?

choices.text: Its composition changed, forming new matter with a new color
Nothing: a change in color is always a physical change
choices.why: Chemical changes are often accompanied by physical changes, because new matter has new physical properties. A color change doesn't rule out a chemical change.

choices.text: Color is a chemical property, so the change is chemical
choices.why: Color is a physical property. The change is chemical because the composition changed, not because the color did.

choices.text: Any change that involves heating is a chemical change
choices.why: Heating can also cause physical changes, such as melting a solid. The test is whether new forms of matter are made.

explanation: The marshmallow burns, so its chemical composition changes and new forms of matter are made. Chemical changes are frequently accompanied by physical changes, because the new matter has different physical properties.

prompt: Chemistry recognizes two types of substances. What are they?

choices.text: Elements and compounds
Metals and nonmetals
choices.why: Metals and nonmetals are ways of describing elements. Compounds are substances too.

choices.text: Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures
choices.why: These are the two types of mixtures. A mixture is a combination of more than one substance, not a single substance.

choices.text: Solids and liquids
choices.why: Solid and liquid are phases, which are physical properties, not types of substances.

explanation: A substance has the same physical and chemical properties throughout. Chemistry recognizes two types: elements, which can't be broken down by ordinary chemical means, and compounds, which are combinations of more than one element.

prompt: Which of these is not a substance?

choices.text: Salt water
Sodium chloride
choices.why: Sodium chloride (table salt) is a compound, and a compound is a substance.

choices.text: Water
choices.why: Water is a compound, and a compound is a substance.

choices.text: Iron
choices.why: Iron is an element, and an element is a substance.

explanation: Salt water is a mixture: salt dissolved in water. A mixture is a physical combination of more than one substance, so it is not itself a substance.

prompt: Which of these is an element?

choices.text: Gold
Water
choices.why: Water is a compound, a combination of more than one element.

choices.text: Sodium chloride
choices.why: Sodium chloride is a compound, a combination of more than one element.

choices.text: Penicillin
choices.why: Penicillin is a compound, a combination of more than one element.

explanation: Gold is an element, the simplest type of chemical substance: it cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means. Water, sodium chloride, and penicillin are compounds.

prompt: When a certain substance is heated, a chemical change breaks it down into two simpler substances. What kind of matter was the original substance?

choices.text: A compound
An element
choices.why: An element is the simplest type of substance. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means.

choices.text: A homogeneous mixture
choices.why: A mixture is a combination of more than one substance. The original sample was a single substance.

choices.text: A heterogeneous mixture
choices.why: A heterogeneous mixture contains substances you can easily tell apart. The original sample was a single substance.

explanation: A substance that can be broken down into simpler substances is a compound, a combination of more than one element. An element cannot be broken down by ordinary chemical means.

prompt: Only 118 elements are known, but over 50 million compounds are known. How can there be so many more compounds than elements?

choices.text: Elements can combine into compounds in many different ways
Each compound contains every one of the 118 elements
choices.why: A compound is a combination of more than one element. It doesn't need to contain every element.

choices.text: A single element can form many compounds on its own
choices.why: A compound must contain more than one element. One element by itself is just that element.

choices.text: Any physical blend of elements counts as a new compound
choices.why: Physically mixing elements makes a mixture, not a compound. Mixtures are physical combinations of substances.

explanation: A compound is a combination of more than one element. With 118 elements to choose from, the elements can combine in a huge number of different ways, giving over 50 million known compounds.

prompt: Sample A is two elements stirred together, each keeping its own properties. Sample B is the same two elements combined into a single substance whose properties are unlike either element. How should A and B be classified?

choices.text: A is a mixture; B is a compound
A is a compound; B is a mixture
choices.why: This is reversed. A is only a physical combination, while B is a single new substance with its own properties.

choices.text: Both are compounds, since both contain two elements
choices.why: Containing more than one element isn't enough. In A the elements are only physically combined and keep their own properties.

choices.text: Both are mixtures, since both contain two elements
choices.why: B is a single substance with properties different from its elements, which is what a compound is.

explanation: A mixture is a physical combination of more than one substance. A compound is a combination of elements that behaves as a completely different substance, with properties unlike those of its elements.

prompt: What is another name for a homogeneous mixture?

choices.text: A solution
A compound
choices.why: A compound is a single substance made of more than one element. A homogeneous mixture contains two or more substances.

choices.text: A pure substance
choices.why: A homogeneous mixture behaves like a single substance, but it really contains two or more substances.

choices.text: A heterogeneous mixture
choices.why: That is the other type of mixture, in which you can easily tell that more than one substance is present.

explanation: A homogeneous mixture is so intimately mixed that it behaves as a single substance. Another word for a homogeneous mixture is a solution.

prompt: Which of these is a homogeneous mixture?

choices.text: Alcohol stirred into water, forming one clear liquid
Ice cubes floating in liquid water
choices.why: Ice and liquid water are the same substance in two phases, so this isn't a mixture of different substances.

choices.text: A layer of oil floating on top of water
choices.why: You can easily see the oil and the water as separate layers, so this is a heterogeneous mixture.

choices.text: A glass of pure water with nothing added
choices.why: Pure water is a single substance, a compound, not a mixture.

explanation: When alcohol and water mix into one clear liquid, you can't tell by looking that two substances are present. A mixture that behaves as a single substance is a homogeneous mixture.

prompt: Which statement is true of heterogeneous and homogeneous mixtures alike?

choices.text: They are physical combinations of two or more substances
You can tell the substances apart by looking
choices.why: That is true only of heterogeneous mixtures. A homogeneous mixture looks like a single substance.

choices.text: They behave as if they were a single substance
choices.why: That is true only of homogeneous mixtures. In a heterogeneous mixture you can tell the substances apart.

choices.text: Their substances join to form a new substance
choices.why: Forming a new substance with its own properties describes a compound, not a mixture.

explanation: Every mixture is a physical combination of more than one substance. The two types differ only in how intimately the substances are mixed.

prompt: A student stirs sugar into a glass of pure water until it all dissolves, then drops in a few small pieces of pure iron, which sink to the bottom. How many different substances does the glass now contain?
explanation: Three: sugar, water, and iron. The dissolved sugar is still present even though you can't see it, because dissolving forms a homogeneous mixture rather than a new substance.

prompt: An element is a yellow powder. A lump of it shatters when struck with a hammer, and electricity does not flow through it. How should it be classified?

choices.text: A nonmetal, because it is brittle and a poor conductor
A metal, because it is a solid at room temperature
choices.why: Nonmetals can be solids too. A metal would be shiny and malleable and would conduct electricity well.

choices.text: A semi-metal, because it is a solid but is not shiny
choices.why: Semi-metals have some properties of metals and some of nonmetals. This element shows no metal properties at all.

choices.text: A metal, because hammering can break it into pieces
choices.why: Metals are malleable: hammering flattens them into thin sheets. Shattering means the element is brittle, a nonmetal property.

explanation: A nonmetal is brittle when solid and does not conduct electricity or heat very well. This element shatters and doesn't conduct electricity, so it is a nonmetal.

prompt: An element is shiny and conducts electricity, but it is brittle and shatters when hammered. How is it best classified?

choices.text: A semi-metal
A metal
choices.why: A metal is malleable and would flatten into a sheet when hammered. Being brittle is a nonmetal property.

choices.text: A nonmetal
choices.why: Being shiny and conducting electricity are metal properties, which nonmetals lack.

choices.text: A mixture of two elements
choices.why: The sample is a single element, not a mixture. Elements with properties of both metals and nonmetals have their own name.

explanation: This element has some metal properties (shiny, conducts electricity) and a nonmetal property (brittle). Elements with properties of both metals and nonmetals are called semi-metals, or metalloids.

prompt: A jeweler hammers a small piece of metal into a thin sheet. Which term describes what happened?

choices.text: A physical change
A chemical change
choices.why: Only the metal's shape changed. It is still the same metal, with the same chemical composition.

choices.text: A physical property
choices.why: Being able to be hammered into sheets is a property of the metal, but the hammering itself is a change: the metal's shape changed.

choices.text: A chemical property
choices.why: A chemical property describes how matter changes form in the presence of other matter. No new matter formed here.

explanation: The metal's shape changed, but its chemical composition did not, so hammering it into a sheet is a physical change.

prompt: Electrical wires are made by drawing a metal out into long, thin strands. Which pair of metal properties makes metal wire possible and useful for carrying electricity?

choices.text: Ductility and good electrical conductivity
Malleability and good electrical conductivity
choices.why: Malleability is being able to be pounded into thin sheets. Being drawn into thin wires is ductility.

choices.text: Ductility and brittleness
choices.why: Brittleness is a property of nonmetals, not metals. A brittle wire would snap instead of bending.

choices.text: Malleability and a shiny, silvery color
choices.why: Neither of these is about wires or electricity. Malleability is about thin sheets, and shine doesn't help carry electricity.

explanation: Ductility is the ability to be drawn into thin wires, and metals conduct electricity well. Together these properties make metal wires possible and useful.
